MIDSTREAM REPORT CARD

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
More than 6 months later, the FG Landfill is still operating. We give the DEA a report card.

Unique Selling Point:
Three months after the Minister of Environmental Affairs was due to make a decision on the future of the FG Landfill site in Midrand, the dump is still operating unhindered. It's unclear what the holdup is, while two new reports show that the complaints of nearby residents of respiratory problems and eye irritation are not unfounded.
We give the DEA a report card for their handling of this matter.

Summary:
In March, we reported on the community in Midrand's battle against the FG Landfill site, a large general waste dump owned by Interwaste. Residents complain of the bad odours and gases emanating from the dump and health effects such as respiratory problems, eye irritation and nausea.
In February, the Department of Environmental Affairs issued a directive to Interwaste to close the FG Landfill site. But Interwaste appealed to the minister of environmental affairs and the directive was suspended pending the minister's decision.
Submissions could be made until end March and the minister then had to make a decision within 90 days. But no decision has been made as yet.
Interwaste and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development are also still embroiled in a court case over the waste dump's licence.
But in the meantime it's business as usual at the dump and the residents say things are worse than ever for them.
The DEA has since commissioned two new reports. One models the air dispersion of the hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide released from the dump. The other report examines the health effects of residents' possible exposure to hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide.
The air dispersion modelling report found that the average limit (DEA standards) of sulphur dioxide could possibly be exceeded within up to 600 m from the site and limits of hydrogen sulphide (WHO standards) within up to 419 m of the dump. It shows the gases could reach the southern boundary of the Midstream Estates in very low concentrations but would reach Glen Austin residents in high concentrations.
The health effects report found that the sulphur dioxide concentrations were low and the health effects insignificant. But the levels of hydrogen sulphide were often high enough to cause eye irritations and respiratory effects in residents nearby and even complaints of headaches and nausea "can not be regarded as invalid". The odour threshold was also frequently exceeded.

Further information:
The two reports were leaked to us and are not in the public domain yet.
The air dispersion modelling report laments the lack of data supplied by Interwaste, which did not supply real measurements of the release of gases at its site. Estimates had to be used.
It also suggests that monitoring should ideally be done over a period of at least a year to get accurate results. The measurements the report was based on, was taken over two and a half months (76 days).

Press Release:


Months after the Green Scorpions clamped down on a landfill, there seems to be little change for Midrand residents who still complain of respiratory problems and headaches. After years of trying to get authorities to take action, a new report now validates residents’ claims that the air they breathe could be making them sick. Carte Blanche scores the Department of Environmental Affairs and the minister.

Script:


VO: In March this year, we reported on the battle between the FG Landfill in Midrand, between Johannesburg and Pretoria, and its neighbours, who believe air pollution from the dump affects their health and quality of life.

STRAP: CARTE BLANCHE, MARCH 2017: DR PHIL MAHUMA: Last night I woke up at half past one coughing and choking, because of the air.

STRAP: CARTE BLANCHE, MARCH 2017: STEPHEN PRETORIUS: We get terrible headaches...I’ve sealed the door. I’ve siliconed it on the outside and it’s even varnished, to seal it from coming in.

VO: In February, the Department of Environmental Affairs or DEA’s Green Scorpions ordered the owner of the landfill, waste management company Interwaste, to close it down.

STRAP: CARTE BLANCHE, MARCH 2017: GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: We’ve done extensive investigations – at all times of the day and night … we’ve got the evidence.

VO: We returned to check on developments. The order to close the landfill was suspended because Interwaste appealed to Environmental Affairs Minister Edna Molewa. Meanwhile, FG Landfill keeps going.

CLAIRE MAWISA: So since we’ve been here six months ago, has there been any change?

STEPHEN PRETORIUS, MIDRAND RESIDENT: It’s exactly the same.

VO: Stephen Pretorius and his family live across the road from the landfill.

STEPHEN PRETORIUS, MIDRAND RESIDENT: The Green Scorpions go in and they close them down and they just continue operating.

VO: Family physician Dr Phil Mahuma lives about two kilometers away, in the Midlands Estate.

DR PHIL MAHUMA, FAMILY PHYSICIAN: The residents are becoming angrier and despondent and I think they are now in a state of shock.

STEPHEN PRETORIUS, MIDRAND RESIDENT: I believe Green Scorpions have been back there and doing inspections, but the conditions are still the same.

VO: The DEA hired independent experts to analyse hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide levels measured between April and June just north of the landfill. They couldn’t verify Interwaste’s own numbers. Using weather data, the DEA experts said it is plausible that the most likely sources of hydrogen sulphide would be located at the FG Landfill. The sulphur dioxide likely originates elsewhere. The report showed that gases may travel in low concentrations as far as the south of Midstream Estates, where Mahuma lives.

DR PHIL MAHUMA, FAMILY PHYSICIAN: I drive from town and when I reach a certain radius you can feel the lips stinging, your eyes stinging. Sometimes there can be blurred vision. This is not normal.

VO: The DEA’s health experts validated some of the residents’ health complaints. Their report said that the concentrations of SO2 were low and posed no health risk, but the H2S was a different matter.

STEPHEN PRETORIUS, MIDRAND RESIDENT: Periodically I need to go away to the bush to clear my system, because it builds up and it builds up and it gets to a stage I have constant headaches. I have constant nausea. My throat is unbearable. And when I go away, it takes about a week then it starts getting better.

VO: The report said some people may get headaches and nausea when the hourly average of H2S is above 50 micrograms per cubic metre of air -- and above 150, there’s a real concern. In the 76 days checked, there were 32 occasions when the H2S level was above 150 micrograms, sometimes for as long as 4 hours.

CLAIRE MAWISA: Some residents we spoke to when we were last here have actually left the area and moved away from Midstream.

STEPHEN PRETORIUS, MIDRAND RESIDENT: I’m the next one. I can’t take it anymore. I think Green Scorpions do what they can, but I think their hands are chopped off. On the ground level things are happening and they’re doing a lot of work, but it seems that it doesn’t get carried through.

VO: The DEA declined to respond, saying that the matter is still under consideration and there’s currently nothing to report on. The Green Scorpions deserve credit for continuing with their work, so they get a C.

CLAIRE MAWISA: You’ve written personally to the minister. How would you score the minister?

DR PHIL MAHUMA, FAMILY PHYSICIAN: As far as this problem is concerned, I would give her an F. She’s really failed us. I think she could have done something.

VO: The Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, or GDARD, is also fighting a battle against Interwaste over the landfill’s licence.

VO: The law does not prevent landfills from being in residential areas but they must ensure there’s no danger to health or the environment and no nuisance caused to anyone.

VO: After some delays, GDARD will have its day in court in December to challenge the licence, which it said expired in 2015, after four years. GDARD wants the company to reapply, but Interwaste maintains its licence is still valid and had no expiry date. GDARD is persistent, but there’s no result yet, so it gets a D.

VO: Interwaste maintains that the DEA’s directive was issued unlawfully and without evidence. It says the FG Landfill has state-of-the-art landfill liners installed, it’s expanded the landfill gas management system and it recently scored 97% in an independent audit.

VO: Interwaste told us in writing that the reports and the ambient air quality monitoring “have not verified or concluded that the FG Landfill is the primary or only source of emissions”.

DR PHIL MAHUMA, FAMILY PHYSICIAN: I think to be fair, the smells are different. At around 1 o’clock we get the musty smell and towards early morning at around 4 o’clock you get like chemical smells. So actually, we can tell the different smells...

VO: Residents and the authorities report little change. Interwaste gets a below-average E.
The authorities and the company at the centre of this battle failed the community.

PROMOS
10 secs
Months after the Green Scorpions clamped down on a landfill, there’s little change for Midrand residents who still complain of health problems … why is there no solution?

15 secs
After years of trying to get authorities to take action, a new report backs Midrand residents who say the air they breathe, makes them sick.
STEPHEN PRETORIUS, MIDRAND RESIDENT: It builds up and it builds up and it gets to a stage I have constant headaches. I have constant nausea. My throat is unbearable.

15 secs
Why do investigations and directives by the Green Scorpions to close a controversial landfill in Midrand seem to go nowhere?
DR PHIL MAHUMA, FAMILY PHYSICIAN: The residents are becoming angrier and despondent and I think they are now in a state of shock.

But the levels of hydrogen sulphide were often high enough to cause eye irritations and respiratory effects in residents nearby and even complaints of headaches and nausea "can not be regarded as invalid". The odour threshold was also frequently exceeded.
metadata.Further information: The two reports were leaked to us and are not in the public domain yet. The air dispersion modelling report laments the lack of data supplied by Interwaste, which did not supply real measurements of the release of gases at its site. Estimates had to be used. It also suggests that monitoring should ideally be done over a period of at least a year to get accurate results. The measurements the report was based on, was taken over two and a half months (76 days).
